comment_text.value:
That is not quite the same problem. Modern browsers are vastly more standards-compliant than they were in the IE era, and most CSS/JS works across Chrome, Firefox and Safari without browser-specific hacks.

There was a time when we routinely did browser sniffing, maintained IE-specific code paths, used vendor prefixes everywhere, and sometimes shipped completely different fixes depending on the browser. That largely disappeared as browsers converged on standards.

Chrome-first development can still cause bugs elsewhere, but that's usually a "testing/implementation problem" rather than the same compatibility mess we had back then.

comment_text.value:
There seems to be a bit of a gap vis a vis solutions in the article - someone could set the system up so it doesn't incentivise tanking. The punishment for tanking should be that the teams performed poorly for no compensation. It's all very well to set up a system to encourage poor behaviour then shame the people who behave rationally. But it is much more sustainable in the long term to make good behaviour also strategically optimal.

> Post-Hinkie, the league experimented with variations of the lottery, but none of them could deter teams from losing on purpose.

I struggle to believe they've tried everything unless they're also talking about players betting against themselves (which probably is impossible to overcome without bans). Incentives aren't easy things but there has to be some system where winning > losing.

On that topic we're actually pretty lucky - in the real world, the winning strategy over long time-frames is almost always talking, prosperity and cooperation. Not obvious why the powers that be are so keen to involve other strategies that routinely deliver worse material and moral results.

comment_text.value:
Co-founder and COO of OpenRouter here.

Thanks everyone for the feedback here. Some of this we are aware of, some of it we aren't. Some we can fix, some of it is inherent to inference (and we in fact improve the situation dramatically).

Philosophically, at OpenRouter we are trying to do two different things, that are sometimes at odds with one another:

1. Let you use a lot of capacity across a lot of providers, in a way that "just works" and you don't need to worry about it.

2. Have a huge variety of inference available so you can pick radically different price/performance tradeoffs, data policy decisions, geographic destinations, inventive hardware, etc.

These are inherently odd bedfellows, and we are still very much improving how we can make both of them true at the same time.

Some quick thoughts on the article itself:

1. Benchmarks: YES! Providers benchmark differently. We run benchmarks on the live endpoints continuously, monitor the median performance, and kick providers out of the default routing pool if they vary by more than a standard deviation. We work hard (and continue to invest) to make sure that providers serving sub-par inference can't game the system, and that our routing actively avoids them. So the chart is accurate (it's our chart) and it actively influences our routing decisions!

2. That is bad and we will fix it. Sorry.

3. When we on-board providers we run essentially the same test as the author did to verify that the param is working as expected. If it isn't, we don't launch the provider. However this is not one we are running constantly in production. We are working on making this more robust in general and I do believe is fundamentally solvable in a way where it will "just work".

4. We 100% agree that users should not filter by quantization. It's a bit of a legacy concept in general; there is a huge amount of code between "model weights" and "inference API" and in almost all cases quality degrades in that part of the stack, NOT in the model weights themselves.

5. Hmm...we will dig in here. We monitor tool calls in real time and route around providers that are regularly mis-parsing tool calls. So you should get a very low rate of these in general. Another area we have invested a lot in: https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/auto-exacto

6. We will dig in here as well. I'm surprised this is happening frequently enough to be noticeable. We eat the cost when the finish reason is an error, but not when it is "stop". Perhaps we can expand our "insurance" program: https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/zero-completion-i...

7. Will investigate.

8. We attempt to heal these, but obviously missed some. Will fix.

9. We do not rate limit by IP. Would love some more information here, as that is very surprising.

10. Ugh. That sucks. I'm sorry. We are introducing QoS tiers for production apps, which will address a lot of this.

story_title.value: So you want to use OpenRouter?

comment_text.value:
> Dead code removal is unexpected by the programmer, because programmer does not write dead code.

Dead code elimination is like the single most profitable optimization in the compiler, especially in conjunction with inlining and constant propagation that makes several branches become trivially dead. And its removal is very much expected by programmers, because (for example) bounds checking tends to work by generating bounds checks for every possible array access and relying on the compiler to be able to prove most of those bounds checks redundant.

No, my suspicion is you're actually only against certain kinds of dead code removal, but the kinds you're against are so inconsistent that it's impossible to implement a decision program except by including a routine to read the programmer's mind.

comment_text.value:
Maybe don't take words out of my mouth. I studied math when I was younger, and got to the top 0.001% in mathematics competitions. Why did I study so hard? In order:

1. I recognized that understanding math had incredibly profitable applications.

2. It was a sport.

3. It was a hobby.

Do I think the world will look the same when math is "solved"? Absolutely not! And we're seeing it transform right before our eyes. I routinely ask Claude, "here's the general idea for a math/cs/ai problem I'm working on, can you help me figure out the maths? oh and then implement it too."

Could I figure this out myself? Of course. Having the idea is halfway to formalizing it in math. But I remember even last year working on GPU kernels by hand and having a bunch of little arithmetic or indexing errors burn me, because I'm just slower and less perfect at doing the math correctly. Now I basically just tell Claude, "go optimize a GPU kernel for this problem". I still have to tell it what to look out for (architectural, algorithmic, memory improvements), but I'm sure the next model won't even need that.

story_title.value: What should we tell our students?

comment_text.value:
> My solution was to create a weekly "team meeting" from 8am to 11am every Friday and invite all of them to it.

I've been part of these and the focus time is nice.

It doesn't address the root problem, though. If engineers are being bombarded with meetings, those meetings just get squished into the afternoon time slot.

The secondary problem was that some people started treating the blocked-out time as their only work time. Once that dedicated block came to an end, they mentally switched out of work mode and were not going to do any more work until the next morning. Before all of the "nobody can do more than 3 hours of good work per day" replies, this was a real problem because people also used this time for discussion things with each other on the team, actual team meetings, and various things other than heads-down work, leaving less than the allotted time for actually working. It was also a problem when something would come up at 2:30PM and the person responsible would defer it to next morning's work session instead of taking an hour to do the work. This might all sound like minor annoyances and it was only some people doing it, but the theme repeated itself so much that many of us soured on the idea over time.

The bigger problem was that it didn't address the real issue. Every situation is different and in my case the manager was part of the problem. His solution to everything and answer to every question was to get two people talking. He thought of himself as a switchboard, routing people to other people on our team.

Blocking out meeting time helped a little, but what we really needed was an active manager who was handling communications himself and only bringing the team in when needed. We also needed him to have our backs when we declined meetings or asked if they could be an e-mail.

The healthier managers I've had take a constant, active interest in keeping their teams' meeting workloads down and rooting out interruptions and distractions. They also empower their team to forward meeting requests to the manager to evaluate and ask that external requests at least cc them for visibility. Every time I've had a manager like that, I haven't felt the need for blocked out focus time.

story_title.value: Sorry, I'm in a meeting

comment_text.value:
I think there's a middle position, too. I'm a software guy and a lot of my house is automated. But unlike the non-software tech enthusiasts I know, my automation has some strict guardrails. Like it does not rely on the cloud (in fact is not allowed to communicate with it), local only. And every device must fail back into no worse a state than the manual equivalent. E.g. the door locks are electronic, but still have a knob for the deadbolt and a key on the outside. The light switches are all momentary switches but if the controller fails they fail to just being plain switches.

But ... I kinda feel the sentiment, I routinely joke (and feels like less of a joke every year) that when I retire in a few years, I'm removing every last computer from my life.

If I seriously needed a classifier, I would just train my own and it would run on an iPhone. Any CTO worth their salt would suggest the same, because it's not even remotely comparable to training a large language model (w.r.t. compute or training data required).

comment_text.value:
A major limitation of directly using "System 1 decision models" (a.k.a., logistic regression, and related uncalibrated classifiers over the output/logit space) in enterprise settings (or other high-stakes settings) is that such estimators are not reliable estimators of the predictive uncertainty in the presence of covariate shifts, and such estimators also lack a means of instance-wise data attribution (i.e., interpretability-by-exemplar), so they're not the ideal estimator for verification, routing, uncertainty over retrieval and tool-calls, etc.

For decision-making with neural networks, we instead need the older idea of estimators of the predictive uncertainty with constraints in the feature-representation space (over training/support of the estimator), as with Similarity-Distance-Magnitude estimators: https://pypi.org/project/reexpress-sdm/

comment_text.value:
Show HN: SV Premium – Compare infrastructure prices at your actual usage

Hi HN, I built https://svpremium.dev after two migrations cut our infrastructure bills far more than I expected.

DNS: ~$150K → ~$5K/year. We’d used NS1 for years, initially for advanced features like filter chains. As we moved our infrastructure to anycast, we ended up mostly using basic DNS and geo routing. But we were still on an annual, prepaid contract sized for peak capacity. Trying to right-size it and remove features only got the quote down to around $100K. We moved to Route 53; our expected bill is around $5K/year.

Images: ~90% cheaper. Devs picked imgix because it was easy and free to try and integrate. As our user-generated content grew, so did the bill: under its old pricing, unique origin images accounted for about 80% of the cost. Moving to Bunny eliminated that charge and reduced bandwidth costs, cutting the total by roughly 90%.

Servers: Of course, everyone knows that hyperscalers (AWS/GCP/Azure) $$$ > DigitalOcean/Vultr $$ > Hetzner $

What vendors am I missing? And where is the familiar, expensive choice worth the premium - and why?

The concept of the website is basically showing the Sillicon Valley / Big Tech / Enterprise premium you're paying for when there's plenty more of options.

story_title.value: Show HN: The safe-choice tax – what the vendor nobody gets fired for costs

This started when I spent twenty minutes trying to figure out whether Squeezits still exist (they don't - discontinued 2001). "Do they still make ..." turns out to be something everyone Googles, and the answers live in dead forum threads.

So I built a memorial: ~239 products so far, each with its lifespan, what killed it, and one verified odd fact (PB Max was reportedly killed despite ~$50M in sales because the owners disliked peanut butter). There's a "Gone or Still Here?" quiz - harder than it sounds, things keep resurrecting - and a random button.

Stack: Python static-site generator, JSON data, GitHub → Netlify. The content pipeline is the part I find interesting: AI-assisted research (Claude Code with a custom skill that mandates web fact-checking), but nothing publishes without passing a human review gate - early on the AI claimed a snack had been revived when it hadn't, which is exactly why the gate exists. In this niche, accuracy is the product: two weeks post-launch, Google is already routing question-clusters like "when were cheese nips discontinued" to the relevant page.

Happy to answer anything about the build or the model (boring long-game SEO + ads, in the spirit of odd single-purpose sites like IMCDB). And tell me what you miss - I'll research and add it.

comment_text.value:
> The same-machine-multi-user security paradigm has been dead for a long time.

I ... what? Huge swaths of the computing landscape depend entirely that model. Schools (from primary to academic research), Windows Active Directory workplaces, thousands of cheap VPS providers ... the list is very long. All of those contexts absolutely use user accounts on the same running OS kernel as a security boundary. I've seen more than a few academic and government worksites where effectively radioactive data owned by one user was on the physical machine that other users routinely used--just not in an account they could access. Those places' infosec history wasn't perfect, but not because of the insider-threat-on-shared-machine risk.

In cloud/webtech, I think it's easy to overlook just how many massive organizations rely on stuff like shared AD workstations, cheap user-based shared hosting, or shared HPC a la "every member of the university gets an account on the SLURM cluster and we slice compute allocations by account--and separate accounts prevent the new intern from seeing protected IP".

Like, malicious employees can attack such systems, yes. But with adequate mitigations (network partitioning, internet access control, auditing/telemetry, good SEIM, user data encryption where appropriate, patching...all the usual good practices) this is a perfectly viable security model. Not perfect, but nothing's perfectly secure and every security paradigm has tradeoffs.

Those environments aren't dinosaurs or asking for a security disaster; they've made considered risk assessments and decided that the multi-user-machine security model works for them.

comment_text.value:
"Bad" is subjective, but as I stated, it's my opinion. It's not about work ethic at all; it's about your own values.

To simplify:

1. Reinforced behaviors become stronger, while others get weaker. Ultimately, I'm a behaviorist (ACT).

2. Work is a big part of your waking life.

3. If you spend that much of your life going through the motions, you're strengthening behaviors that may not be constructive.

4. When your situation changes, and you need those more constructive skills and behaviors, you may find them much more difficult to access.

That's a very functional lens. However, there's a deeper lens you can apply. I believe people feel most fulfilled when they're routinely acting in alignment with their core values (what they truly care about).

Phoning it in at work may actually be "workable" from an ACT standpoint if your personal life lights up all your values, and you are feeling completely fulfilled by friends, family, hobbies, etc.

However, I would venture that most people also want to feel that their work is giving them some feeling of intrinsic satisfaction, not just a paycheck. You can call it Purpose, Mission, Self-Efficacy, whatever you want. In my framing, people don't want to live in conflict with their values 8 hours/day.

But there's an even more basic argument that I would make: Life is incredibly short. You are hurtling toward death. If you're phoning it in, you're giving away your most precious resource for a small amount of financial security (and you still might get fired). You may find that when you hit 45 (or 65) you look back and weep for the decades you poured into something that you didn't care about, or even held in contempt.

You have to do what's right for you, but it's never too late. As someone who has admittedly phoned it in previously, I'm violently on the other side now. Regardless of how you feel about your job, I strongly recommend finding a way to give a shit, or getting out by any means necessary.

Hey guys,

If you've used Claude Tag, you know the potential of it for orchestration, a few months ago I built a version of it as a Claude Code plugin, that brings the concept as a local version of it, simply as a always-on task driven Claude Code agent. Our clis, our local memory, our filesystem, our tools, for you or your team.

It's how I manage and orchestrate several projects across different companies, and how I've been running always-on agents since. Set one up under 5m, it's just Claude Code so you can run with any subscription including 20$, it's fully customizable and it has got some magic focused on token efficiency using claude code native features:

1. Chat through Claude Code channels (Discord, Telegram, iMessage etc). Handle permission prompts in chat, recalls past conversations, keeps per-channel rules ("remember this for this channel"), has per-user allowlists for teams, and you manage the session from chat: !model, !effort, !clear, !compact, !stop, etc.

comment_text.value:
> You responded to a 40-word comment just there.

And if it was the only one it wouldn't even deserve a comment. But it isn't because basically any mention of DNSSEC triggers your insistence that it can't work. All the stuff you've commended which didn't work went unmourned, but DNSSEC you're really animated about.

> The Internet has worked just fine without a centralized PKI for DNS name signatures for decades.

The Internet likewise worked "just fine" without a secure shell for decades. Tatu shipped his ssh command in 1995. Before that, and indeed for a year or five after as it was popularized, it was routine to rlogin to remote Unix machines - the user's unencrypted password was just sent over the wire like it's no big deal. But I'm going to guess that Thomas the Security Guy doesn't think rlogin is good enough in 2026 does he?

> Key pinning isn't a thing anymore because we have Certificate Transparency

Mozilla removed Key Pinning in Firefox 78. They added CT checks in Firefox 135. Hopefully it's pretty obvious to you that 135 was not before 78. HTTP Key Pinning was a fiasco. CT is to some extent coincidental timing rather than somehow a planned replacement and doesn't even attempt to address the same problems, because many of them were mirages.

> The gun, in the case of the domain name system, points the other direction.

Not at all. Browser vendor choices impact on the DNS and not vice versa. It's been that way since the beginning. The browsers don't look for the modern HTTP service record in DNS, so just make an A record for www to create a web server. And when they did finally decide to use HTTPS records they decided how to use them and when to use them, there was no way for DNS to impose that.

This is exactly the approach we've been taking with Metal Gear Solid. We’ve been working on a fork of mgs_reversing (which is targeting 100% matching decompilation of MGS Integral) to bring the game natively to microcontrollers: https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/mgs_reversing

Instead of high-level emulation, the decompiled C source is compiled directly to Xtensa machine code for the ESP32-S3. We replaced the PlayStation SDK/GPU/GTE with custom software routines, running on a DIY handheld built around a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense.

To speed up development without constantly flashing hardware, we run the compiled firmware image directly inside a browser-based hardware simulator CLI (velxio-cli) to verify serial outputs and execution in seconds.

Having 100% matching C code makes native ports to embedded platforms completely feasible without relying on heavy JIT/interpreter glue.

comment_text.value:
This is an interesting question! I'm not an expert in Orleans but I have looked at it alongside koka. The user defined key vs pid distinction is important and using a user defined key like in Orleans has advantages for keeping track of their virtual actors(grains). Their automatic lifecycle management is nice, but you really have to trust the runtime to know when something is really idle. I think their failure handling with auto state restoration is a mistake, recreating an actor with bad state is a recipe for crashes.

What I have that Orleans is missing is compile time protocol checking, typesd and hash checked remote calls, capability management, cluster authentication, and no stop the world GC. Orleans doesn't have choreography per se, they have sagas as a convention.

Yeah, GO routines are meant to solve different problems than share nothing actors.

comment_text.value:
> If you're not under pressure to vibe code for work, and you still like writing the code, I don't understand this sentiment.

We don't necessarily like writing the code by hand, but those of us in this situation don't really have a choice and it pays the bills (handsomely, I might add; not complaining at all).

Every line of code has the entire organization behind it due to requirements that cannot budge an inch. There's also lots of rigorous manual testing beyond what is already automated. The automation efforts for this kind of software, sometimes going on decades, has left no stone unturned yet lots of human work (and payroll cost) remains.

This is what a real business looks like once it's settled into its competitive niche, and I'm routinely surprised how many devs on HN are not in this kind of role. Those people who are forced to lean hard on AI are at the highest risk of unemployment, and I have to assume they're either junior or made a lot of questionable career choices.

story_title.value: Living in the Weimar Era of Ruby

Leased lines, MPLS, custom routing setups, hell just a VPN that fails closed. There are so many options for doing this, all more secure that just slapping a device online behind whatever router the cheapest ISP gave you.

A quick search puts the list price of the touchscreen-equipped controller at around €7,000 [1]. So this is hardly the typical dirt-cheap IoT device you can buy for a few bucks from China. The product label also says "Made in Denmark."

comment_text.value:
This is very well done and applies to lots more electronics than copy machines, and lots more corporations than Xerox.

You could substitute a laptop computer for a copy machine, as an example of another electronic hardware/software purpose-built assembly, and lots of the same things will naturally apply, even if the nominal use of the laptop never includes any need to open it up for routine electronic service for the lifetime of the device.

IOW even if the only thing anybody "services" is the software.

Lots of people would also agree that the ideal in either case would be no routine service needed at all, not even the software. For the lifetime of the device, of course.

It doesn't take that much additional abstraction to relate how so many companies should really reckon with the possibility that people having great experience on the front line also often have just plain natural leadership ability. Even if it has been untapped it could still amount to more sound decision-making, compared to executives in the same company having less of both.

Even if there is not some star performer on the front line who would make any executive seem dumb by comparison, the combined experience and leadership abilities of all those front-line people are still sometimes going to put the combined executives to shame if given the chance.

Hence why they are not usually given the chance.

story_title.value: The soul of maintaining a new machine

comment_text.value:
I think we're now moving a bit far afield from my original comment, so I'll try to get us back. I'll give an example of how Berger's Marxism leads him astray. He called the Impressionist's work "bourgeois nostalgic art", art for the elite. But the Impressionists were the exact opposite of art for the elite, they were revolutionaries against elite, academic art based on patronage. They painted for the public and the market, and their work showed (for what was the first time), ordinary people enjoying themselves in routine settings like a picnic or a restaurant.

Why does ideology force Berger to diss their work and minimize how popular and well-liked they were? Because they showed ordinary people enjoying themselves in the first mass society in the world in ordinary everyday settings. But Marxism says ordinary everyday society is oppressive and the people ground down by a brutal capitalist elite. He can't get himself to understand that Western European everyday life of the late nineteenth century was the best life ever for ordinary people anywhere in the world or anywhere in history, and the fact that they were out happily enjoying it in a civilized urban way was a new thing in the world, and depicting that was an important advance in art.

story_title.value: Chapter 1 of "Ways of Seeing" by John Berger (1972)

comment_text.value:
Rayhunter is a great tool, but unfortunately, it is only a passive monitor for cellular state changes and not an active defense.

Modern Stingrays / IMSI catchers support all standards up to 5G. They easily exploit 4G networks and 5G Non-Standalone (NSA) deployments. The only effective active defenses include (a) using a device locked strictly to 5G Standalone (SA) mode with SUCI (Subscription Concealed Identifier) enabled, preventing fallback to 4G/3G/2G where identity spoofing is trivial, (b) keeping the device in airplane mode most of the time, only going online briefly from unpredictable, shifting locations, and (c) using custom cellular baseband firmware that can reject anomalies (like a tower suddenly appearing too close or lacking neighbor cell lists), though this requires custom building your own solution as ready-made consumer solutions are hard to find. The last one can be achieved with Rayhunter, of course, but it would require some patching to Rayhunter and always carrying a mobile phone connected to the Rayhunter-supported Wi-Fi hotspot device.

Finally, intelligence mercenaries (and therefore LE agencies that contract them) use warrantless network-side exploits like SS7/Diameter attacks to remotely query the core telecom routing system and harvest the location of the tower target's phone is currently using¹ ². This doesn't even require sending legal DD requests to telcos to get target's cell tower.

[1] https://www.researchgate.net/publication/370809133_Attacks_t...

[2] https://www.lighthousereports.com/methodology/surveillance-s...

story_title.value: Feds got warrants to use fake cell towers to hunt down Don Lemon's producer

comment_text.value:
When I was little, like 10 years old, I was obsessed with reading when not in school. Also I had a lot of insomniac nighttime hours to deal with. And my parents got wise to leaving the light on in my bedroom, or the classic TV-ploy, "flashlight under the covers". So, in an attempt to fool them, I would bring my favorite tome into the bathroom, where they routinely left the light on all night, and I'd slip into the dry bathtub, and read to my heart's content. And I believe that this went on for some time until they figured out or called my bluff. They considered it weird and quirky that I'd chosen that route, but I really needed my books.

Later in my teenage years, I would be spending inordinate time in the bathroom every evening, with a tub of Vaseline. That's right, I was able to solve a lubricated, optimized Rubik's Cube in 63 seconds!

comment_text.value:
> Its probable that AI will roll out much faster ...

I think a sort of acceptance is the real problem.

Just like because of convenience/laziness people will give up against surveillance, I think the same thing will happen with AI.

I have been listening to the book "talking to strangers" by malcolm gladwell

The book is about how people don't understand others.

One point was that people "default to truth" when listening to other people. Basically people default to believe what others are telling them, and it is good for society. But it can be terrible with accomplished liars, specifically liars who seem confident they are telling the truth. He had examples of CIA spies, Hitler and more.

Wow - I was thinking about AI while listening. AI sounds convincing. It doesn't give hints that it might not be telling you the truth. It will confidently give you answers all day long.

The only way to counteract this is to be a critical, pedantic person. But to behave this way is counter to the rules of society. Folks who routinely do this range from unpopular to completely shunned by society. Think about being critical about adtech instead of shrugging it and accepting it.

sigh.

comment_text.value:
Well, the end product might be similar, but the approach is a bit different. 'xc' is a language in its own right, and it can be compiled (with xcc) to both the CPU and GPU (and I have plans to make it work on a Zynq too, a sort of HLS).

The C front-end I'm currently working on is something that looks at the LLVM IR that clang produces and converts it to xc-IR, then runs the data-parallel extraction through the same routines as the original xc language. Consider it to be a 'Y' branch on the inputs - you can feed it LLVM IR or xc source code, they both get convered to xc-IR and from then onwards it's all the same.

So yes, you get tiled work-units, overlapping in time between compute/data-transport and tuned so that actually works, and an opportunistic scheduler that sends them to whatever worker can handle it at the instant of being sent. That opportunistic nature means the faster cards (eg my 5080) will naturally get more work, because the scheduler just keeps all cards busy. The divide between the 5080 and the 3090 in my Windows test box is about 2:1.

But the scheduler is also aware of networked GPUs - my M4 max has a pretty fast GPU, but it's connected to my wife's M3 Max by thunderbolt, and I measured a 37 Gbit/sec connection, so my app can send data to be processed over that very fast link and get results back. If you have a 10GBit nic, then it will work pretty well too, if your nic is "only" 1Gbit then modern GPU speed means that unless your work-units are really computationally intensive, it'll be faster to do it locally - and xcd will work that out at runtime and adopt that faster approach.

story_title.value: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?

comment_text.value:
Here's a helpful diagram:

    Politics   <--------- Left ------ Center ------ Right ---------->
               |                         |       Neoliberalism      |
    Economics  |     Anti-capitalism     |        Capitalism        |
    US         |                      DSA    Democrats  Republicans |  
    Germany    |                  SPD           CDU/CSU         AfD |
    UK         |                    Greens     Labor  Tories Reform |           
    France     |              LFI           Renaissance          RN |
There are some general observations one can make:

1. The far-right parties are linked and coordinated and generally funded by very wealthy people;

2. The rise of far right parties is a direct result of declining material conditions;

3. Far right parties get to blame immigration and trans people because, in general, there is no counterbalance to that narrative blaming the actual cause: capitalism and ever-increasing income and wealth inequality;

4. The "moderate" (which really means centrist or center-right parties) will predictably and routinely ally with far-right parties to crush any leftist momentum. As an aside, the term "moderate" is intentionally conflated by pollsters, politicians and the media and really means nothing;

5. The topic of economics is typically avoided in most Western countries because the economics are indefensible. Instead you have manufactured wedge issues to divide people such as immigraiton, gay rights and the existence of a handful of trans people. This suits both major parties in most countries because they're both neoliberal, which is to say that they are uniparty on defending capitalism;

6. People will defend capitalism and attack socialism without knowing what either of those things are. Ask someone what capitalism is and you'll usually get a hand-wavy claim about "free markets" or even just "markets", which isn't true at all. No markets are free and markets exist in every economic system. Some of our earliest writings from 4000+ years ago are about market transactions.

So when you see things like protests in France, the rise of Reform in the UK and the rise of AfD (as well as others such as in Italy) know that it's all related and has the same root cause.

Fascism is capitalism in crisis. We saw how that worked out in the 1930s in the wake of the Great Depression. In the US, FDR was forced to make concessions to the working class to stave off the perceived threat of communism. In Germany we got Hitler. And after WW2, the US went on an imperialism frenzy, imperialism being the highest form of capitalism.

All of this is only going to get worse until we address the core issue, which is capitalism.

So when you see things like protests in France, the rise of Reform in the UK and the rise of AfD (as well as others such as in Italy) know that it's all related and has the same root cause.

Fascism is capitalism in crisis. We saw how that worked out in the 1930s in the wake of the Great Depression. In the US, FDR was forced to make concessions to the working class to stave off the perceived threat of communism. In Germany we got Hitler. And after WW2, the US went on an imperialism frenzy, imperialism being the highest form of capitalism.

All of this is only going to get worse until we address the core issue, which is capitalism.

comment_text.value:
This is basically correct but there is some nuance. First of all, people working on unoriginal or very small scope stuff, such as app clones or ad hoc analyses in notebooks, will never hit that wall. They'll never even know the wall is there. This is a bit annoying, because they then generalize their experience with toy projects and come away with the mistaken belief that anyone could make anything if only given enough tokens. This is most problematic when they are in leadership positions.

However, the real value is in complex, non-trivial, and above all novel code. This has been true for a long time, and it's just as true in open source as it is in industry or academia. Here, agents are far less useful. In fact, the only people I've seen have any kind of success using agents on these kinds of "serious" projects are people who are already serious programmers. They already know how to design and test stuff, they already know how to supervise junior developers, they already have an intuition for which aspects of the project the can safely delegate to a less experienced developer. So they're able to use agents as a "better autocomplete" in their own code, or use it to flesh out the non-essential and more routine aspects of the project, or even just delegate the agents to the role of code reviewer.

Here's the thing though. The less experienced ones, the people who don't already have those skills, they do get burned when they "stick the fork in the socket," as you put it, or in other words when they try to use agents to take on projects they don't fully understand... but they don't learn anything! The ones I've seen, anyway. Relying on agents insulates you from the code, which also prevents you from building a mental model of what's going on under the hood, which in turn makes it impossible to learn anything at all. They just keep yelling at the agents, telling them to fix stuff even though each fix introduces yet another regression in an endless loop... they don't know how to dig themselves out of the hole they've dug. And after all, what is the solution? To spend five years down in the code mines, paying your dues as a junior dev, reading and typing and thinking about mere code for the requisite 10,000 hours? Nobody has the time or inclination for that.

Agents, in other words, break the learning loop. You can't learn to program, and therefore can't learn to design or architect software, not really, if you're using agents. I am unfortunately coming to the sad conclusion that the last programmer has already been born; if you didn't have 5+ years of experience and a pretty good handle on the more advanced aspects of programming (such as software architecture, design patterns, optimization, debugging, etc.) before agentic programming became a thing, then I don't see how you ever will.

It'll be like COBOL programmers - the industry will shrink from the top-down, with the first to go being the new college graduates looking to enter the workforce. Inexperienced devs have always been given less interesting projects, but they stuck it out because they were learning valuable skills, building experience, making the economically rational decision to invest in their own career. But anyone entering the market today will never get out of that trench - anyone that actually needs a real programmer for a serious project will hire someone with decades of experience - there will be plenty of supply. And the projects on offer for junior devs won't teach them how to program, only to supervise agents. As a knock-on effect, smart young people already see the writing on the wall and are pivoting to other majors, which just reinforces the trend. This might cause problems in a few decades when all the real programmers start to retire, but when has the market ever considered long term consequences?

story_title.value: It's still ok to enjoy programming

comment_text.value:
define "we".

Because again - I think lots of businesses are already taking a good look at models well off the "cutting edge" because they're good enough for what that business is trying to do. They're already there.

If you're doing categorization, tagging, form-filling, customer support routing, etc... you don't need anywhere close to cutting edge expensive models.

Hell - Jev being so popular is basically exactly that group going "what's the cheapest way we can make this decision".

Meanwhile, there are plenty of spaces where you still want real model improvement. But a lot of traditional business was basically process and paper pushing. You don't need a Phd level model for that, you need an intern level model.

---

But that's the trap for the large providers - intern level models are cheap and easily available with current open weights. It's going to be a very tight market, and margins will go down to essentially the floor (especially once we exit the current constrained-compute market).

Somewhat ironically - the technology itself makes switching costs basically zero. It's not just that there's no big lock in, AI is like an anti-moat. It actively fills in and paves over whatever moat you might have for price conscious customers.

Not to defend this, but don't the police lie to suspects all the time during interrogations? The article doesn't seem to assert that DHS lied to anyone except the suspect (at the time of the detainment), which AFAIK isn't illegal and might even be routine.

comment_text.value:
1. Therefore Stripe is irrelevant and you shouldn't have brought it up in this context.

2. Then USDC is irrelevant and you shouldn't have brought it up in this context.

3. Fees are irrelevant; worldwide is irrelevant; "10 seconds" is the wrong category of speed: throughput rather than duration.

Though 10 seconds isn't even fast in this context, payment cards are routinely used on e.g. the London Underground at the turnstiles, and anything over about 2 seconds would look like an error and that en-masse would cause noticeable queues getting into or out of the system and corresponding city-level commuting delays.

And normal card use in London public transport acts like a smart contract, as the fee isn't known on initial use, but when exiting the transport network later. Similar on hotels, from what I hear, though they handle it differently.

Both of these have a broader problem: anything on credit (which these function like as the final bill isn't known at point of sale) is fundamentally not part of the blockchain system, so even with all that, all credit cards need something bank-like (and if you use a smart contract to simulate this, you're taking on the risk of bugs in the contract).

From what I understand, TfL actually does all the hard work themselves and figures out the bill later, so if their DC went down the same time as Revolut's they'd not work even if this was a crypto solution that solved every other issue.

And normal card use in London public transport acts like a smart contract, as the fee isn't known on initial use, but when exiting the transport network later. Similar on hotels, from what I hear, though they handle it differently.

Both of these have a broader problem: anything on credit (which these function like as the final bill isn't known at point of sale) is fundamentally not part of the blockchain system, so even with all that, all credit cards need something bank-like (and if you use a smart contract to simulate this, you're taking on the risk of bugs in the contract).

From what I understand, TfL actually does all the hard work themselves and figures out the bill later, so if their DC went down the same time as Revolut's they'd not work even if this was a crypto solution that solved every other issue.

In practice that would create even more ineffective veto points that already result in stasis and dysfunction in the US Congress.

For more than a decade the US has been stuck operating by renewing the same budget more or less with minor modifications at random intervals of time depending on the political mood. It always gets approved eventually after occasional pointless, wasteful shutdowns. But nothing actually changes from those veto points, just more routine dysfunction and grandstanding.

Same with debt ceiling. Another veto point that gives leverage but has zero effect on actual spending. It probably sounded like a brilliant idea to control spending in the 70s or whenever it originated. But is entirely ineffective at the purpose of addressing the deficit.

Self expiring legislation would very likely end up the same way. Just another pro forma procedural roadblock that wastes time and makes the legislature even less effective at real problem solving instead of posturing.

comment_text.value:
Fun story time:

Almost a decade ago now, I was a happy, high-functioning alcoholic. Winery tours, Scotch tastings, workplace drinks, etc.

It was all "fine" until I started struggling to get to sleep without a little "nudge"; then it was getting back to sleep in the wee hours; then it was every hour or two, 24x7.

Then I decided to go cold turkey while on vacation in Hawaii with my family, because who wants to be the drunk asshole in search of a cocktail while everyone else is having a good, sober time at the beach?

Boom: detox seizures, ER visit, and the ever-so-helpful prescription of Ativan so I wouldn't seize again. I was discharged with the instructions to "take as needed, up to every four hours." Since I was an addict in pain, I took that to mean, "take them every four hours, or maybe more often."

Cut forward 3-4 days, and the scrip ran out. Boom: more DTs, this time from the benzos.

It wasn't long after that when I went through my first inpatient psych visit b/c I was in no way equipped to handle withdrawals from two highly-addictive drugs at the same time.

Sadly it took another couple of years and another trip through the ER + inpatient care before I realized that doctors would and did prescribe me meds that were actively harmful in the interest of short-term comfort.

It's been six years since the last big episode and I'm genuinely grateful I only threatened myself with my shitty brain chemistry (however aggravated by poor medical intervention) rather than putting other people at risk. It could have been much worse if, say, I routinely drove people around or did any kind of safety-critical work.

Regardless: benzos are not "lightweight" drugs, and giving them to people with any kind of history of substance abuse disorders is a Bad Idea.

story_title.value: The Other Epidemic: Trying to get off benzodiazepines

comment_text.value:
I was often really frustrated with my parents pushing me to learn at least some basics on the piano. Why do I have to practice, I want to watch Dragonball Z. Practicing is sooooo boring. Ugh.

I'm still not amazing at piano. But having a basic understanding of musical theory, understanding how a lot of these concepts of harmonics and tones and waves are related, have really unlocked a lot of neat things throughout my life. Their push for me to learn an instrument drove me to performing for family events including a couple of weddings, with my involvement in their day still quite a powerful shared memory between us. It led me to learn additional musical instruments, which I enjoyed a lot more than piano. It helped me in other artistic endeavors like theater. It helped me understand music production, something I moonlight in as a volunteer. It gave me instant connections with lots of people who were important people in my life but probably would have forever been passing strangers. It has given me something else to share with my children, as they routinely ask me to play for them and show them how instruments work. A basic understanding of waves and harmonics and what not even helped me understand a lot of more complicated EE topics.

Learning an instrument early in my life was definitely a powerful and deeply impactful thing in my life journey, almost entirely positively outside of many afternoons where I had to catch up on DBZ later.

comment_text.value:
The prescription of benzos to help with things like sleep is wild to me. There are certainly use cases where they are extremely helpful but just like anything the lack of nuance is where things get shitty.

I wonder how many anxiety sufferers would jump on the option to be completely free of their misery in exchange for a 1 hr mandatory daily exercise routine that can be done entirely indoors. I was a complete shitshow until I started rowing at least 10km every morning (365 days per year).

There was a time when this level of exertion sounded insane to me. The unfortunate reality is that this is the bare minimum my particular physiology requires to achieve the desired outcomes. I suspect the threshold isnt that far off for some others. It took me half a lifetime to get used to the idea of exerting myself like this for at least an hour every single day.

There are days where it feels very hard to get going, but then I recall the alternative options and their consequences. That's all it takes for me now. I've been to the bottom of a few rabbit holes. I know how those stories end.

comment_text.value:
Well, I honestly believe it is rank incompetence. Speaking as someone who's monthly electronic GST filings, commercial authentications, and digital payments, i.e. continued livelihood, is beholden to cert and PKI authorities like eMudhra having their shit together...

As for the odds of this being state-sponsored... It depends on the state's incentive, weighed against its continued behaviour, over the last 10-odd years. Everything below is easy to substantiate with citations. There are too many to cite... I put myself at real risk just by stating any of the following under my real name.

  ---My take: Never attribute to malice, what one can to (rank) incompetence.---
I expect eMudhra-esque collossal gaffes, as a normal course of life, stemming from the apathetic, insular, feudal-minded, shoddily run bureaucracies that the majority of our government and quasi-government organisations are.

Basic day-to-day operations being unavailable, because "Sorry sir, site is down." is a normal everyday life experience of their own staff, not to mention the common person. eMudhra is one of that tribe, and I'd say they are not the worst offenders of the lot, by a wide margin. I'd probably give the "best of the worst" title to our national Employee Provident Fund.

Of course, one can't totally rule out nation-state-level stupidity, such as BGP poisoning by the Pakistanis.

  ---Nation-state action: Wither sufficient incentive? ---
If our current federal administration has incentive to do it, they will... And, given their track record, if it does turn out to be nation-state-engineered for short term tactical gains (to hell with the consequences for anyone else), all I will do is sigh and move on with my day. Cornered politicians can go to any length to save their own skin (usually, just to save face)... Collateral damage be damned. Popular examples include world superpowers bombing distant nations, for whatever gain or goal (usually short-term, because well you most probably won't be President a second time (and never a third)), using whatever pretext they can sell to get others to also get behind (the individual's psychological cover in a firing squad, scaled up to many allied powers).

In India, absolute majority governments have amply demonstrated the same failure mode as US heads of state empowered with de-facto fatwa powers, as of the US PATRIOT act. Given motive and incentive, they easily turn the full might of their uncheckable wrath and ire at our constitution, as well as directly at the common public.

You know, like sending out military forces to "calm down" the pesky student protesters acting against "the national interest".

As we speak, massive nationwide student protests have been bringing shame and angst to the government of our ruling party at the centre (BJP and allies), as well as their various governments across states. Many protests have happened at this scale in the last decade+ of the same ruling party's unbroken streak as a majority power in the centre (federal government). Those other protests were like water off a duck's back. The ongoing student protests, for reasons I've not dug into, appear to be a clear and present existential threat to the incumbents.

My gut feeling is... the incumbents aren't passing the electoral vibe check any more.

The sentiment on the streets of the national capital, and large urban centres nationwide---almost entirely comprised of a new crop of young voters (18 y.o. up to early 30s)----is that they feel robbed of an economically viable future. They've organised at scale (millions on the street) with persistence (they are literally owning the "Cockroach" epithet thrown at them by the powers that be). And in short order, material consequence---unprecedented in its decade-long winning streak so far---befell the incumbent party's administration. The Education Minister had to resign, and they've generally lost face with that whole voting-age cohort. Brand-name loss of key leadership is further disrupting their internal party cohesion. Plenty of hopefuls in there, salivating after the top dog position, but thus far too weak to sway the cult following of the public faces of the party. Even an hint of weakness gives the wannabes a real opening to try. Textbook demagoguery.

If that is indeed true, then in their place, I too would seriously worry about losing even more ground in the next national election... It's not far now. Because? "Winning by overwhelming majority" has been the one and only priority of the incumbents, driving all their work post-election (where work includes constitutional shenanigans)... Being a populist party borne of, and cultivated by far-right nationalist ideologues (the RSS and "Sangh" community), with a longstanding desire for religious supremacy (Hindutva and Sanatan dharma), they publicly and loudly dream of a hundred-year golden age. Uh, no, now I think it's become a thousand-year era (really!). That's not totally insane if you're suddenly goated at winning electoral politics, because our head of state can enjoy unlimited tenure. Yes, you heard that right, India has no constitutional limits to number of re-elections to the Big Chair, whether successive or alternating.

Without looking at absolute numbers, I feel confident that the influx of new voters (lots of people can turn 18 in a single government tenure) far outstrips the older ("whatsapp uncle / aunty") voter base that the incumbents pander to. This has been a lucky break for the fumbling Congress party because their legacy name is finally regaining some cachet... The much-mocked Rahul Gandhi presents like someone the young'uns can actually talk to, like a human being.

But the Gandhi-brand Congress were once an absolute majority power too. At which time they suspended our constitution, and weaponised federal agencies, and created the playbooks that all future governments have been able to deploy at various scales. I expect nothing less from any other party that grabs absolute majority. Currently it's the BJP. Tomorrow, it could be anybody else. Thus far, it's been the secular-presenting Congress, followed by the Hindutva-majoritarian BJP. Woe betide us if next the Communist Party of India gets a bite at that juicy apple. 'cause, like, I don't have to explain what that sort of government can do with absolute power. <shudders>

  ---Nation-state action: Whither evidence of having the means and using them with impunity?---
Ref: our liberally interpretable Information Technology Act. Among other things, it enables and empowers arbitrary blanket Internet Shutdowns and Blackouts, by local states as well as national authorities, to "protect the peace". In some deeply conflicted areas, like Jammu and Kashmir, censorship measures under martial law would give both, the Great Firewall of China and the Stasi a run for their money.

Ref: at-scale weaponisation of Pegasus, as of 2021. Federal and even state authorities like police departments have weaponised nation-state electronic warfare technology with impunity. Usual suspects / targets are politically inconvenient individuals and groups... opposition politicians, bureaucrats with a spine or conscience, students, media, artists, NGOs etc...

All this mixes badly with pre-existing supercharged Sedition laws. These effectively obviate habeus corpus, and are routinely used to prosecute speech interpreted as anti-national / seditious under the generous ambit of our IT laws (we don't have a real privacy law). Mere suspicion and/or fear and/or dislike + Pegasus + garbage IT laws = authority can brazenly plant incriminating evidence on your device... it's reportedly been done multiple times.

People have been held in prison for less (just inconvenient speech), without possibility of bail, for months and years on end, without trial. The main goal is to cause irreparable reputational damage, to create future deterrence... It's pretty effective. A secondary goal is to take the stubborn ones off the board, with no legal recourse, until they break. And of course, to permanently defang the truly outspoken and indomitable few... Some of those people have been in high-security federal prison for years on end now.

It depends. In Ontario (or at least Toronto where I live), the fire department and ambulance services are separate. The paramedics are chronically underfunded and the result is that the fire department is constantly running up milage on multiple expensive and massive fire trucks for routine calls that should just have been a paramedic. This also compounds traffic issues when they park at their destination.

It makes sense for them to automatically show up for some situations (eg car accidents), but there should be a properly funded triage system.

Same goes for the police, which are often called for situations where there should be some other social workers available (again, there are exceptions where police should also be present in those situations).

As with many dependencies, I wholeheartedly question the requirement and relentlessly cut them out without replacement.

Taking the definition from another user on this comment-chain:

"an OpenAI compatible endpoint routing across multiple providers based on latency"

If the endpoint is truly OpenAI compatible, you can just switch out the vendor by switching out the HTTP address, we are talking potentially about a single line change.

- LLM_HOST = "api.openai.com" + LLM_HOST = "api.competitor.com"

It sounds silly, but remember that software is a winner-takes all game, 99% of devs will lose, so if you are seeing 99% of devs do the same thing, it isn't surprising that it's a grossly wrong choice. It takes skill and guts to be in the 1%, reject the mainstream trends, and just write code without grasping at external imports to do even the most basic things.

I'd like to take this opportunity to sell out, I'm open for contracts if you are looking for a remote 1% dev. Early stage startups only, email in userpage.

comment_text.value:
Nope; the compiler was supposed to end coding; when the word coding referred to taking an abstract program written on paper and translating it to machine code.

Compilers were first called automatic coders.

The word compiling referred to something more like linking: producing an image containing multiple library routines. In other words, similar to compiling an anthology of works into a book.

After compilers, the word coding to changed to writing program code in any language.

Because the tooling for automatic coding also compiled the bits of code into a larger image, the term compiler/compiling came to be used for the coding part also.

While the terms reshuffled, the concrete reality was simply that people worked less in assembly language, not that fewer people worked or that programming ended.

I think there’s a lot of value in a “stack skill” like this offers. I don’t personally buy that the scaffolding around “markdown source of truth” makes sense; I prefer to work as close to the agent harness as possible. An iterative conversation and then “cool, write a doc to memorialize and then build this” usually goes well for me, keeping the back-and-forth in context for as long as possible.

Since most of the comments are just throwing shade, here’s what this is actually doing:

https://rustoffrails.org/docs#the-stack-in-one-breath

>>>

Axum on hyper (the binary is the web server: HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2, no app server or nginx needed)

Tokio · SeaORM (SQLite locally,

Postgres in production, same code)

Tailwind

a frontend mode chosen at birth:

htmx (default): Askama (compile-time checked templates) + htmx. No Node. Optional React or Svelte islands.

inertia: React or Svelte pages with Rails-style server routing, via a generated Inertia adapter. The default when you want a JS UI.

spa: a Vite SPA (React Router or SvelteKit in SPA mode) + a JSON API.

api: no UI, for mobile backends and public APIs (in progress).

comment_text.value:
> Sometimes people who don't actually understand the law make spurious claims that those investors are legally required as fiduciaries to put their funds into the highest yielding investments. But in reality there is no such requirement

The requirement is what a lawyer can convince a dozen jurors the requirement should be. If there's a lawsuit against a fund manager at an institutional investor saying "you didn't fulfill your duty as a fiduciary because x", there's at least some risk that x becomes a real responsibility for fiduciaries through the outcome of that case. If the zeitgeist dictates that as a responsibility, it is a responsibility.

> They can underweight Meta stock if they believe it's overvalued due to potential legal risks or corporate governance problems or whatever.

The fact that they aren't doing so when the company is losing billions of dollars in legal judgments would suggest either

1) They can't do so because they would lose money doing so

or

2) Our system is in need of reform so that when executives direct a company in such a way that it is routinely facing legal exposure, shareholders remove those executives so that corporations act as better citizens and things are handled at the shareholder meeting level instead of the court system level.

comment_text.value:
Alan Kay (of Smalltalk fame) has a similar, related explanation: computing is a pop culture with little regard for the past (https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/bbm:978-3-319-90008-7/...). There are thousands, maybe millions, of developers who have little knowledge of the history of our field. I’ve found this true even of graduates from highly-ranked computer science bachelor’s programs. Think of all of the current-day LLM researchers and engineers who have never heard of Minsky, McCarthy, Lisp machines, and other aspects of the history of AI before we learned that attention was all we needed.

It wouldn’t surprise me if Apple’s UI/UX teams are staffed with people who have never heard of Don Norman, Bruce Tognazzini, Bill Atkinson, Andy Hertzfeld, Susan Kare, Larry Tesler, and other pioneering figures who contributed to Apple’s legendary 1980s and 1990s software.

It’s a lack of onboarding and knowledge transfer, combined with an Eternal September of thousands new CS grads being constantly produced annually, who are sadly not being taught enough history of computing at their universities.

My dream as a CS professor is to help rectify this, at least amongst my students.

Alan Kay (of Smalltalk fame) has a similar, related explanation: computing is a pop culture with little regard for the past (https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/bbm:978-3-319-90008-7/...). There are thousands, maybe millions, of developers who have little knowledge of the history of our field. I’ve found this true even of graduates from highly-ranked computer science bachelor’s programs. Think of all of the current-day LLM researchers and engineers who have never heard of Minsky, McCarthy, Lisp machines, and other aspects of the history of AI before we learned that attention was all we needed.

It wouldn’t surprise me if Apple’s UI/UX teams are staffed with people who have never heard of Don Norman, Bruce Tognazzini, Bill Atkinson, Andy Hertzfeld, Susan Kare, Larry Tesler, and other pioneering figures who contributed to Apple’s legendary 1980s and 1990s software.

It’s a lack of onboarding and knowledge transfer, combined with an Eternal September of thousands new CS grads being constantly produced annually, who are sadly not being taught enough history of computing at their universities.

My dream as a CS professor is to help rectify this, at least amongst my students.
hits.story_title: No more icons in every menu by default

You have a point but it's just hyperbole in the other direction. Yes, Rust is only a small fraction of the code in use every day, but it has nonetheless achieved deep penetration into critical infrastructure.

Cloudflare's network routing code is predominantly Rust. Massive parts of AWS and Azure are Rust (including crown jewels like S3 and Lambda). Multiple car manufacturers have shipping Rust code in their production cars for years, albeit yes it's a slow process intoroducing it into regulated industries. Airbus and Boeing are putting up job openings for Rust development. As mentioned critical pieces of Windows and Android are now written in Rust. If you use Discord - that's Rust. If you use Amazon Prime Video or Disney+, that's Rust. I could go on.

When like 40% of internet traffic and 75% of end user devices are using Rust in some capacity, to say that it's "not production" is just ignorant, arrogant nonsense.

> There are places in the US where the criminal justice system would break down if every defendant refused a plea deal and demanded a speedy trial

I'm actually not aware of any place in the US that routinely administers what could be considered a speedy trial. It's a shame, really, but perhaps an inevitable side-effect of the ever-increasing burden on the part of the prosecution. Pre-Warren Court, it was normal for criminal cases to take days between arrest and trial.

> Our jails are full because we have unnecessarily long sentences and a prison system that is meant to be punitive instead of rehabilitative

I make the point in a sibling comment that the US actually has lower incarceration rates compared to its peer nations, relative to their homicide rates. Our jails are full because we have a lot more crime. We can agree to disagree on the "root causes" thereof.

comment_text.value:
Not the point.

C++ provides quite a broad set of features for concurrency support (https://cppreference.com/cpp/thread). The task-based paradigm (i.e. promise/future etc.) is a logical framework which is rather confusing to folks who come from a straight thread-based (think pthreads) background.

Raymond Chen in his own inimitable style makes things clear so one can see that the logical task-based framework is nothing more than a higher level abstraction above thread-based core routines i.e. there is no underlying magic involved.

Using the task-based api makes your code clearer and portable since you are dealing with only logical dataflows amongst your problem-domain "tasks" and not any underlying OS/thread-library/machine level complexities.

story_title.value: C++ futures part 1: The mental model

comment_text.value:
I also want to briefly note that communicating, from the outset, "this is a significant incident, your keys are compromised, the attack is ongoing and you cannot enter new keys as _those too will be compromised_" is a better response than leaving people to figure out the unfortunate combo endpoint of "my keys are compromised, I have rotated them, this has broken my site but I have new keys, and oh surprise, I can't deploy". The full story needed to be communicated more clearly; the email just said "revoke your keys", which I urgently did... and then remembered/found out that changing environment variables requires a deploy.

I would rather have known earlier that I should put a notice on my site, or my own social media, or notify my own customers ASAP and disable some functionality (or make my own choice about porting somewhere else as a mitigation) than get caught out like this after the horse has bolted and it turns out you've been desperately trying to get it back into the paddock for days.

comment_text.value:
I was deposed once.

It was 6 hours where the opposing counsel tried to rattle me / get under my skin with insulting questions.

To be clear, I was only an expert witness in the lawsuit (drug + pregnant lady + birth defects). It paid extremely well, but was something I would never want to do routinely.

At the end of the deposition, the lawyer had to catch a flight to the west coast and she asked ME if I would drive her to the airport* (she said she'd pay me my hourly rate)!

At that point it was clear that the insults were just theater and "part of the job", but I took it all too personally and told her I had to get home.

* She was late for the flight and Uber wasn't a thing yet.

comment_text.value:
At some point we need to have a tough conversation about collective civic engagement and societal dysfunction and not just individually running from it or routing around it. All these institutional problems have been stacking up for the past twenty years, they're only continuing to get worse and worse, and the most common reaction I see from it is some variation on "try to just stay out of its way".

There's a tendency for people to react to institutional problems like this by saying they'll just move over here to a blue state, or they'll monitor their accounts closer on reporting bureaus, or they'll just have a lawyer on retainer, etc, etc. If a legal system in a red state is this dysfunctional, you can't simply hide away in a blue state with better-run systems. The underlying problem - the social decay of much of the US and the broader world - needs to be directly engaged with and confronted.

Redox OS, Asterinax. PD: my first distro was Debian Woody, comparable to Slackware with a 2.2 kernel back in the day, 2.4 was optional. So I've seen everything.

comment_text.value:
isochrone.ch is an interactive web app illustrating public transport accessibility in Switzerland. Pick any starting point and it shows you where you can go within a given amount of time. This is quite useful in a country with such an amazing public transport network where most people don't own a car (people can typically use it to find new hiking or skiing destinations, when searching for a new flat, etc.).

The innovation here is that the transit routing logic runs on the client; I wrote a little open source library (minotor.dev) implementing the RAPTOR algorithm in TypeScript and optimizing timetable data (GTFS from https://opentransportdata.swiss) to be shipped to the browser. This enables super responsive visualizations as no round trips to the server are needed.

I built it on my free time and published the first version early 2025 but kept improving it since then (range query support, altitude filters, memory optimizations, etc.).

comment_text.value:
> Crucially, no routine blood biomarker, lipid metric, or clinical risk score could identify these individuals with inflamed coronary arteries.

I call bs on this. There are two common blood tests that are meant for it:

1) hs-CRP (High-sensitivity CRP)

2) Lp-PLA2: Lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A2 (Lp-PLA2), also known as platelet activating factor Acetylhydrolase, is an inflammatory enzyme that circulates bound mainly to low density lipoproteins and has been found to be localized and enriched in atherosclerotic plaques. In multiple clinical trials, Lp-PLA2 activity has been shown to be an independent predictor of coronary heart disease and stroke in the general population. Measurement of Lp-PLA2 may be used along with traditional cardiovascular risk factor measures for identifying individuals at higher risk of cardiovascular disease events.

I have routinely had both of these blood tests among others, although I paid myself to get them.

As for hs-CRP, it will likely show an elevation. If you use a binary classifier with a higher threshold of what's safe, e.g. 3.0 instead of 1.0, you will miss it! I am guessing this is why they missed it.

comment_text.value:
You said it. Depending on your knowledge of the entity producing the work, you get a different experience. In a vacuum though you'd appreciate the work for it's actual qualities which you find appealing. The potential for appreciation isn't different at all; it's just overruled by stronger feelings regarding the current trend of AI-hate vs AI-love. Like given identical works from 2 humans, if you respect human A and despise human B, then it's a near 100% certainty that you'd appreciate the work attributed to human A and find every possible fault with that attributed to human B. With a fun bit of hypocritic confusion if it's the same work with the attribution going back and forth.

Also the point about humans preferring the unique and "shiny". Human-made things will always be unique (nobody can do the same the the exact same way twice without machine help), while machine-made things are usually not unique but can be made so (and even then a generative routine used to make something unique can be replayed).

story_title.value: Award-winning AI literature

comment_text.value: Hi, question from a sysadmin / network engineer. Why localhost with port forwarding? Why not native mechanism like routing and mdns? I’ve gave Docker and other container managers which do networking the same way a try a few times and I always found the network unnecessarily complicated. Eventually I came across OrbStack which uses the aforementioned mechanisms. Every container gets an IP address in the local bridge and responds to mdsns queries. This plays especially well in “compose” scenario when services on containers can all use original port numbers. And containers can be accessed with hostnames, so there won’t be conflict between port numbers especially if I run multiple composed stacks.

comment_text.value:
> Pace makers, dialysis machines, brake lines.

That’s fair, including insulin pumps over Bluetooth with known vulnerabilities. Many vulnerabilities might be fixed or formally verified if they are part of the architecture.

> Do you know how elevators work now? Their safety mechanisms? Planes are 10x more likely to cause death.

Both rely on inspections, routine maintenance, procedures, and fail-safe hardware afaik. Just like climbing gear.

Would formally verified software add anything? For example, could it cut the need for inspections or software maintenance? I think neither is going to change.

But what might change is that the specific spelling error on an elevator display is formally verified. It becomes about coziness with impressive amounts of paperwork that only a few people can understand.

Just changing one statement requires new verification, which is why formally verified code currently is not touched but ported verbatim into new projects and “rewrites”. That cost may decrease, which is nice but also not nice: the systems you currently want to formally verify are systems you might not want to alter without high friction in the first place.

I’m hopeful it will produce more robust software, and I’m by no means against it, but I’m skeptical of producing more when we might want to produce less.

story_title.value: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale

comment_text.value:
It's a blurry line. When you replace the deck of "bad stuff happens" cards in a solo game with an app that reads them out to you, but the app could have been a deck of cards, which side of the line does that land? What about if the app starts tracking game state for you as well? Game state that could have been tracked with moving tokens around the board, or using dice as counters, but is simpler in the app. Does that cross the line into video-game territory? What if the app tracks hidden game state, doing the job a human GM would need to do. Does that cross the line?

It's very, very fuzzy. Which may be part of why some board game designers chose not to create companion apps. For example, Arydia (designed by Cody Miller and Ira Fay) tracks game state with three large boxes of playing cards, some of which have "B" and "C" versions; the game will routinely tell you that after you defeat such-and-such an enemy, switch NPC-32 into the "B" state. So you take the NPC-32A card out of the active section of the box and put it in the inactive section, and take the NPC-32B card out of the inactive section and put it in the active section. That could have been done with an app, but every time the question of a companion app gets raised on the Arydia forums at BoardGameGeek, the game designers say "We thought about doing an app, but decided it didn't fit with our vision for the game; we wanted it to be purely a board game with physical components." (I'm paraphrasing rather than quoting).

By the way, I highly recommend Arydia if you're into board games with an exploration, adventuring experience. It's the game that has come closest of all the ones I've played to "RPG campaign in board game form". It's got a steep price because of all the physical components included in the game. But my word, is it worth the price if that kind of gameplay is up your alley (and it is very much up mine). You'll get hours and hours of gameplay out of it, and when you're done, you can reset the campaign and play again. You might think "Oh, I'll remember everything from my first playthrough" but the game is long enough that you probably won't remember most of it.

Anyway, enough rambling about one of only 3-4 games I ever rated 10/10 on BGG. We were discussing board game "companion apps", and there are definitely some that I would say "Yeah, that's a video game in board game shape". But I don't buy those, they don't appeal to me, so I really don't remember their names. They definitely exist, though.

story_title.value: I reverse engineered a board game

comment_text.value:
(Card carrying time-nuts member here.)

Yes, I used to have two Cesium standards in my basement, and that allowed me to make FreeBSD the first kernel which could be wrangled to nano-seconds.

These days timekeeping is much more routine and standard hardware, but even if you miss out on LORAN-C and time-by-telephone and leap-seconds, it can still be lots of fun.

Once you get into it, you can look at the log files, call the remote site, and tell them that somebody left the door to the server room open again.

How ?

A temperature difference of 1°C more or less translates to a 1PPM shift (one microsecond per second) in the kind of crystals used for modern motherboard clock chains.

Most air-con systems will oscillate a couple of degrees with approx 20minute period (gentlemen: Tune your PLLs), so a sudden 5 PPM excursion is either a broken air-con or a door left open.

One of the most amazing feats of applied time-nuttery was Steven J. Murdochs work on fingerprinting the timezone of remote servers, based on their TCP sequences numbers.

(Amongst other things, he found out that a lot of Tor nodes were most probably located in north-eastern USA.)

https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1180405.1180410

story_title.value: Time Nuts (2005)

comment_text.value:
The timeline is wild.

It started on the 20th. When they paused builds again at 2am I was still awake from dealing with this and started migrating to a competitor.

There are about 11hrs between when they confirmed Very Bad reads and notifying customers. But it was ~24 hours after they realized someone had some privilege escalation from their build infra.

My mind is boggled by their response.

If someone is trying to get in, literally anyone can point three or four agents at every attack surface and get your shit locked down. To be just fully under attack for... 48 hours? I can't imagine the situation to just be sitting there and taking it.

I told someone half joking that this seemed like they'd been compromised because it was the only thing that made sense. I wonder why google deleted their whole account earlier this year but all the trouble I've had with them I start to wonder less.

story_title.value: Preliminary Report Oct 21st Security Incident
